This research establishes that the class of valid compositeness judgments for classical propositional logic can be precisely described using the modal logic $Ktp$. We then examine variations of compositeness notions tailored to other normal modal logics, classifying these as either positive or negative compositeness, depending on the original logic $K$. These vibrations can be mathematically represented by a set of coupled differential equations, which often take the form of a generalized Jacobi matrix.  This paper examines the general properties of these localized modes in coupled systems, focusing on their survival characteristics. Adversarial Networks (GANs) can be utilized as generative models for time-series data, particularly sequences in the form of images, videos, and other structured data. In contrast, the use of GANs for unstructured, one-dimensional time-series data, such as temperature and financial datasets, has not been extensively explored. Our study suggests novel architectures for GANs in an unsupervised setting, which can effectively generate high-quality sequences from unstructured time-series data. Our findings indicate that these models excel in forecasting future values within the sequence and significantly outperform baseline methods. Notably, our best model achieved a mean absolute percentage error of 2.54% in forecasting 24 hours ahead on a widely used dataset, which is just 0.03% higher than the best error found using the baseline methods, indicating that these architectures have immense potential in time-series applications.

agnetism is reexamined to accommodate a specific type of non-radiative energy that is present in interacting systems. The approach results in a modified Maxwell equation and an additional energy contribution in Gauss's law, both of which are conserved and have physical justifications. The new theory is then applied to determine the energy associated with the electric field produced by two charged particles, which yields an additional component of energy that is proportional to the product of the charges and the inverse square of the distance between them. Analyzing how these distributions change in simulations that include primordial perturbations, we find that the typical behavior is well-represented by a Poisson process. However, at high redshifts, before the universe becomes transparent, the typical fluctuations diverge beyond what a Poisson process can model. We demonstrate that this early excess corresponds to fluctuations in the density of the cosmic web and has an impact on the accretion rates of galaxies and black holes. Interestingly, we discover that this effect is delayed in simulations that include primordial perturbations by around 10-20 times the horizon scale, which also happens to be the scale at which the excess begins. Furthermore, we observe that this excess diminishes over time as the universe transitions from a matter-dominated to a dark energy-dominated era and find that its amplitude is approximately equal to the density of the cosmic web multiplied by the Hubble constant, which is now very small, around 10^-3.

The geometry we focus on represents a gravitational system that includes a black hole and an electric field in ten-dimensional type IIA string theory. The system is then simplified to its lowest energy modes in the direction of the quasiperiodicity, which allows us to analyze the holographic dual of the corresponding 1+1-dimensional boundary theory. The dual of this boundary theory involves a 1+1-dimensional gravitational system that includes a dilaton and an axion that parameterize the duality orbit of the 11-dimensional M-theory. This study derives closed-form expressions for the mean and variance of the JPDA estimator, making it possible to analyze its performance theoretically. in unsupervised learning with numerous applications.  Despite being well-established, the underlying principles of clustering are not thoroughly understood, which is not surprising given the complexities of real-world data.  To address this, we propose a framework called cooperative learning that views clustering as a series of localized interactions between data points.  This framework is built on the idea that similar data points interact more strongly and is demonstrated to apply to a range of clustering algorithms, including k-means, hierarchical clustering, and even deep clustering.  To take advantage of the underlying structure in the data, we develop a method called localized optimization, which focuses on finding the best subset of neighboring data points.  By combining localized optimization with feedback mechanisms, we create two types of cooperative learning strategies.  The first type is marker-based, which relies on designated reference points to facilitate clustering.  The second type is marker-less, which uses a default protocol to determine the cluster for each data point.  We show that both types can achieve better results than traditional clustering algorithms.  To make clustering more scalable, we develop a hierarchical learning algorithm based on localized optimization and feedback mechanisms.  To evaluate our framework, we create a range of clusterability metrics and use them to compare the performance of different clustering algorithms.  Our experiments show that our framework achieves better results than traditional clustering algorithms.

To address this limitation, researchers have typically considered M-dwarf stars with the lowest levels of magnetic activity, assuming their activity levels remain stable over time. In contrast, this study reveals that M-dwarf stars may experience drastic fluctuations in magnetic activity due to emerging groups of magnetic features that can suddenly bridge and merge to facilitate magnetic reconnection, releasing massive amounts of energy. These findings have implications for future exoplanet detection missions, suggesting that targets with the lowest levels of magnetic activity may not remain stable over time, potentially affecting the interpretation of future transit and radial velocity surveys.

We assess the possibility of using quasiequilibrium solutions of binary black hole metrics to identify patterns that could be linked to quantum properties.  To this end, we developed a method for predicting the behavior of binary black hole mergers based on such patterns.  By applying this method to a specific class of binary black hole mergers, for example with equal mass and spin parameters, we created a predictive model that forecasts the index of the radial component of the Einstein field equations immediately before the merger. The model further reveals that quantum effects become more apparent in the gravitational wave signal as the spin of the black holes increases.  This is in line with previous findings based on numerical relativity. peratures is often achieved through a layer of normal metals that absorb radiation and operate as a heat reservoir at a lower temperature.  However, this method is impractical when trying to cool particles deeper than the neutron star or white dwarf main sequences.  It has been previously suggested that anti-ferromagnetic semiconductors could potentially cool to these low temperatures without the need for a heat reservoir, based on an analogy between their magnetization and the entropy of a heat reservoir.  We argue that this method is more general, applying to any system where a change in a fundamental symmetry corresponds to a change in entropy, and could be used to cool particles deep into the quantum degenerate regime using a linear resistor-like device.  Furthermore, we propose that this technique could also be used to concentrate a beam of light with an extremely high intensity of photons, potentially creating a linear lens.  We also show that this method can be reversed, allowing a change in the average value of a fundamental symmetry to result in a change in the number of particles carrying that symmetry, which we call an anti-tagged anti-matter engine, offering a new possibility for the detection of dark matter particles.

is a computationally expensive process that often hinders the development and training of machine learning models. A promising approach to mitigate this challenge involves leveraging a smaller, high-accuracy labeled subset as a guide to label the larger dataset. This paper introduces a new theoretical framework, which subordinates the large-scale labeling process to the smaller supervised subset. Specifically, the paper establishes a connection between the labeled mini-batch accuracy of a proxy model and the underlying data distribution. This connection forms the basis for a query-based model, which addresses the large-scale labeling problem by categorizing data instances based on the labels of a reference model trained on the smaller supervised subset. A related framework, known as the supervised selector framework, is also described. This involves using a proxy model to select representative samples from the larger dataset, which are then labeled and used to update the reference model. These two approaches are distinct yet complementary categories of methods within the supervised selector framework. Such techniques have the potential to streamline machine learning development and accelerate the discovery of computationally efficient and accurate models.

This is the first time such a robust algorithm has been created for this problem. This is the first time such a fair algorithm has been created for this problem. This research also explores lower bounds for robust algorithms and establishes that any robust algorithm must use $O(n^2)$ space or face a significant decrease in performance. As a result, we propose and study a variant of the minimum sum of squares problem known as the minimum sum of weights problem. This variant has significant implications as many problems can be reduced to it. For this variant, we establish that any robust algorithm must use $O(n^2)$ space or face a significant decrease in performance. This

The, typically short-lived, variations in these surveys' observations at the field level are particularly useful in accomplishing this. These variations can be analyzed over time to gather information on transient phenomena such as supernovae, giant stars, and other celestial events. In addition, studying the correlations between these phenomena and their host stars is crucial for interpreting the results of future surveys. Unfortunately, the vast amount of data generated by these surveys makes manual analysis impractical. In order to build an accurate and high-performance prediction model for labeling the contents of these datasets manually, our proposed approach called StarLoader balances the diversity of the data by applying a set of techniques such as random sampling, removing duplicates, and reducing the number of attributes. This balance allows us to leverage existing catalog data to train a more accurate model than would be possible with the full dataset. Furthermore, we developed a method called StarFormatter to prepare the catalog data for use in training a classification model. This method is particularly useful in situations where the necessary annotations are not feasible to obtain on a large scale. To evaluate our proposed approach, we used the StarLoader framework to train and test a set of models on the example use case of predicting the likelihood that a celestial object is a star.

This is particularly evident in quantum field theories with multiple scales of symmetry breaking, where it is typically necessary to resort to approximate methods such as systematic expansions in the ratio of certain parameters.  In a recent study, we developed a method of perturbative quantum field theory that allows for an exact treatment of interactions and correlations, utilizing a novel ensemble of statistical variations as counters that automatically maintain the symmetry of the system with no need for parameter tuning.  This method was applied to a specific quantum field theory representing the interplay between magnetic interactions and the quantum effects of electron spins.  Using this method, we were able to derive a new series of mathematical expressions governing the system's behavior, demonstrating how they compare to existing approximations and revealing notable differences.  Notably, the exact treatment reveals a distinctive phenomenon – the emergence of a gap in the system's excitation spectrum that arises from a counter that appears in the exact expansion and is missed in the approximate approaches.  The predicted gap in the systems studied should be observable through experimental techniques such as electron spin resonance and X-ray scattering.

F), lepton number plays a significant role in particle physics, particularly in scenarios that involve or minimize neutrino masses. Many beyond Standard Model (SM) theories, including those that involve a singlet or multiplet of leptonically interacting particles, often utilize lepton number as a fundamental symmetry or pseudo-symmetry to construct their neutrino mass formulas. As a result, understanding the underlying lepton number structure is crucial for inferring information about the neutrino mass matrix and the underlying theory. This review will focus on systematically examining all possible lepton number combinations within each of the three generations in order to determine the minimal set of operators that can result in a given neutrino mass matrix. We will then use this approach to investigate three fundamental questions regarding lepton number: its survival, symmetry, or anti-symmetry. We will also explore the underlying physics responsible for the complex and intricate lepton number structure that we observe in nature.

in understanding the dynamics of quantum systems whose environment exhibits memory properties.  Developing practical methods to measure the non-Markovianity of open quantum systems is highly sought after, yet thus far, there is a lack of universally applicable metrics.  This shortcoming is attributed to the fact that commonly used methods are insightful only when specific conditions are met, such as for exponential decay or memory patterns in the time-evolved observables or system density matrices.  We address this challenge by investigating two novel metrics: the first involves measuring the non-Markovianity through a deviation of the reduced density matrix's time-evolution from Markovian behavior, and the second examines the time-evolution of a specific observable in a system consisting of two non-interacting parts.  Our findings demonstrate, using a system consisting of a two-level atom and different types of environments, that both proposed methods provide valuable insights into the non-Markovian characteristics of a system, offering a more comprehensive understanding than methods focusing on specific quantities alone.

Given a quantum circuit describing a mixed state unitary transformation U, our algorithm can identify the functional relationship between inputs and outputs by examining specific output bits. to analyze the behavior of a Markov chain with a stochastic network that varies over time. We are particularly interested in identifying subsets of states that have substantial impact on the chain's behavior. algorithm called FastFT that is relevant to information theorists working on the Shannon source coding theorem. We demonstrate that any source with a finite entropy rate can be perfectly compressed using a compact codebook with a size equal to the rate. The FastFT method is analogous to greedy algorithm alternatives like FT+ and FT-, but with a key difference: it can handle sources with unknown, general probability distributions. We show that FastFT's performance is nearly optimal compared to the best possible lossless compression, achieving a close bound on the rate it uses. We also highlight the practical applications of FastFT, including compressing images, sounds, and text, and compare its results to those of established compression tools like DEFLATE.

We introduce a new method that utilizes unsupervised action classification and  encourages the separation of videos showing the same action, while maximizing  the contrast between videos showing different actions. inaccuracies in current navigation systems is produced by aerosol particles, which have the ability to delay microwave signals and thereby mask the echoes from the ground. This phenomenon is particularly common in the X-band, which is prone to signal disruption due to the relatively large size of the scattered particles. On the other hand, L-band signals have a lower frequency and therefore are less affected by aerosol particles, which is what makes them more suitable for navigation system implementation. Nevertheless, L-band signals have their own limitations and can be blocked by larger water droplets resulting from certain weather conditions, such as precipitation. In this research, we demonstrate the possibility of employing a dual-frequency approach, combining the advantages of both X-band and L-band technologies. By comparing the delay measurements from these frequencies, we can identify and filter out aerosol-induced delays, effectively eliminating a significant source of measurement noise. This technique is particularly useful for improving the accuracy of microwave remote sensing height measurements.

The (symmetric) double graph $G$ can be formally defined as the symmetric subgraph $(G,e)$, with the set of available subgraphs being denoted as $\\Sigma(G)$. Our objective is to examine the maximum number of distinct symmetric double graphs that can be present within a given graph $G$, and we establish a connection with a well-known problem concerning the evaluation of chromatic polynomials. Our main finding is that determining the maximum number of distinct symmetric double graphs that can appear within a given graph $G$ is equivalent to determining the number of possible homomorphisms to a specific type of graph $K_2$, and for this specific type of graph, the corresponding number of distinct symmetric double graphs can be shown to have a maximum value equal to $2^{n-1}$, where $n$ represents the number of vertices in graph $G$.

olds introduced by Gherardini and Katagiri, which extend the concept of the Euler characteristic to maps between different manifolds that have the same dimension. The Euler characteristic of a manifold can be expressed as the sum of its Euler characteristics for each torsion type. For the projective space of a vector field over a finite field with a prime number of elements, the Euler characteristic, when considered over the same field, is a power of the field's elements, specifically $q^n$. As a result, the Euler characteristic of a manifold that is a product of projective spaces and a finite field will also be a power of the field's elements when the number of projective spaces is equal to the dimension of the manifold. However, there are manifolds where this is not the case, such as the rational projective space of a vector field with more than one vector, which has an Euler characteristic that is the square of the field's elements, $q^2$. The torsion in these manifolds is equivalent to the torsion in the rational projective space of a vector field. Furthermore, any manifold that is a product of the rational projective space of a vector field and another manifold has an Euler characteristic that is a power of the field's elements.

Another concern is rogue agents that deliberately disrupt the evacuation process for personal gain.  In this paper, we address the complex issue of multi-agent forced exit problems by introducing a fundamental forced exit game variant.  We then propose solving the complex forced exit game by breaking it down into multiple simpler sub-games. the early universe could have a significant impact on the development of cosmological structure by hindering gas and matter consolidation via gravitational attraction.  The resistance such fields pose to gravitational waves in the early universe allows us to establish an upper limit on their magnitude in the past.  Based on an analysis of the effect of gravitational waves on the distribution of cosmic chemicals, we calculate this limit to be around nanoteslas at the epoch of chemical element formation.  The duration of the universe's proton-pump was found to be insufficient to increase the amplitude of these fields beyond their limit, set by their effect on chemical element formation.  We connect the universe's proton-pump to a cyclic model of the universe, in which case the universe's proton-pump occurs every $\approx 3\cdot 10^{11}$ years, setting the magnetic field's amplitude at the present day at $\approx 0.3\mu$G.  This has the effect of significantly reducing the amplitude of cosmic chemicals on the scale of superclusters of galaxies.  This overshot of baryons could be observed through the enrichment of heavy elements in the IGM, in a technique that could also be used to investigate the universe's chemical makeup at earlier epochs, such as in the study of the Lyman-alpha forest in the spectra of low redshift quasars.

, organizations are securing their networks with ever-strengthening cryptography, leading to a pressing need to balance cybersecurity and communication efficiency. We acknowledge that cutting-edge cryptography technologies may sometimes impede communication speed, prompting the search for lighter alternatives that maintain similar security. In response, our research introduces Alecia, a novel lightweight encryption framework tailored for Internet of Things (IoT) devices, capable of protecting high-speed data transmissions while minimizing processing requirements. Alecia is built on a unique combination of the Simple Linear Permutation (SLP) design approach and the Finite Field (FF) design approach, offering a range of configurable options that allow for optimal performance and security across various applications. Our research demonstrates that Alecia's lightweight design, utilizing only basic arithmetic operations in the Galois Field, results in superior encryption speeds and smaller code sizes compared to leading lightweight encryption frameworks, including the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) and Lightweight Cipher (LWC). Our experimental results show that Alecia achieves faster encryption speeds (up to 3.25 cycles/byte) and smaller code sizes (down to 3.7 KB) while maintaining similar security levels. Furthermore, our evaluation reveals that Alecia's unique design allows it to be optimized for IoT devices featuring ARM Cortex-M0+, MSP432, and Raspberry Pi processors, making it an attractive solution for IoT communication security applications.

alo connection, the removal of satellite galaxies that lie close to their central counterparts is a common data-cleaning procedure. However, our analysis reveals that this practice introduces a systematic error into measurements of the satellite distribution, resulting in an overabundance of satellites at large radii and a pattern of anisotropy in the two-dimensional satellite density profiles. This anisotropy is particularly pronounced in simulations with resolved stellar halos, where it is attributed to a morphological effect produced by the removal process. To address this issue, we developed an alternative method that removes a similar number of in-plane and out-of-plane satellite pairs, resulting in two-dimensional satellite density profiles that match those observed in the Milky Way. This new approach has a notable impact on constraints related to the satellite distribution, eliminating any requirement for additional physical processes such as satellite destruction or a variable satellite fraction with halo mass. However, it does reveal that simulations with resolved stellar halos provide a tighter constraint on the model's mass ratio between galaxies and their associated halo structures, primarily because this method reduces a systematic error that artificially strengthened this relationship in the standard cleaning procedure.

A virtual twin tree is a connected graph with a bipartite structure, consisting of a root vertex connected to two leaf vertices, with the remaining vertices connected in a linear fashion. A twin tree is a subgraph of a virtual twin tree, consisting of a connected graph with a bipartite structure and a distinct set of vertices. This paper's primary focus is on identifying the recognition complexity of virtual twin trees. It is first demonstrated that general virtual twin trees have a finite set of distinguishing properties. Additionally, specific subcases such as series-reducible virtual twin trees or those with a binary structure can be recognized using a finite set of distinguishing properties. It is also shown that certain subcases such as series-reducible virtual twin trees or those with a binary structure have a finite set of distinguishing properties that can be determined in polynomial time. It is further proven that the most general virtual twin trees do not have a finite set of distinguishing properties and that their recognition complexity is equivalent to that of chordal graphs with a specific property known as the circular order.

This limit on the gravitational constant represents the most precise constraint on this variable, and according to theoretical models of a changing Universe, these limits are more restrictive than any existing constraints set by other methods.

, the Higgs boson may not solely represent the fundamental scalar field.  Instead, it could be a component of a higher-dimensional representation within a symmetry-rich profile.  In such a scenario, where the Higgs system exhibits cubic interactions that transfer symmetry charges, we can apply an equivalent description using a lower-dimensional representation.  Based on the requirement that the Higgs system's cubic interactions are symmetrical, we can establish a set of unitary matrices that facilitate a more concise representation.  By implementing a collective rescaling of the Higgs fields, we can further refine this description and eliminate any redundant parameters.  As a consequence, the resulting model comprises a limited set of fundamental parameters that can be measured through experiments.  In addition, any parameter that can be measured within this framework is guaranteed to possess a direct correlation with the Higgs boson's properties.  For instance, the Higgs boson's coupling to electrons or quarks is solely dependent on the corresponding unitary matrix and the scalar field's weight in the higher-dimensional representation.  Consequently, any measurement of the Higgs boson, whether through electron or quark interactions, can serve as a direct indicator of the model's fundamental parameters.

Electromagnetic probes of the system allow for the examination of charged carriers' dynamics in relation to the shifting of holographic conductivities.  Calculated coupled Langevin equations reveal that chaos manifests primarily in the relationship between density fluctuations and charge imbalances, with screening capacities playing a key role.  We demonstrate that chaos can be minimal when screening is complete, yet intense chaos emerges under specific conditions of screening at the boundaries and within certain modes.  The presence of a long-wavelength plasma mode influences chaos in a significant way.  The theory is further supported by the calculation of the Lyapunov exponent.  The impact of strain on the system is also conveyed through a lattice model, showing that chaos can be an enduring phenomenon within a range of strain levels.  The interplay between the continuum and lattice descriptions of the system is explored through a corresponding change in the chaos indicator across the two frameworks.

The surface is assumed to be without boundary and the forcing is defined by a function that is piecewise continuous. An important subcase of an SFS is a Mathieu equation, which models systems like those consisting of a membrane with a region of altered elasticity attached to it, and it does so without relying on linear approximation. It is demonstrated that increasing the strength of the forcing will eventually lead to the appearance of a stable, irregularly shaped region, provided that the original point lies within a certain area. Additionally, if the system's parameters satisfy a specific condition, which involves the intersection of two asymptotic paths, an infinite number of stable and unstable regions will be generated through periodic bifurcations due to a flip transversality condition, which is particularly relevant in the case of an irregularly shaped region that arises from a period doubling.

However, mm-Wave signals are highly prone to being blocked by physical obstacles such as walls and human bodies, making it necessary to use directional transmission methods and frequent signal scanning. These attacks involve a lower-security certified individual accessing a higher-security system by misusing its certified program. Our research investigates a specific type of model stealing attack called zero-knowledge learning by a lower-security user who misuses a higher-security teacher model. In this context, we view the teacher model as a linear classifier that a higher-security user has trained using a certified algorithm based on linear regression. Our objective is to ensure that the learning user does not steal the linear weights from the teacher model. To achieve this, we introduce an alternative loss function called robust cross-domain loss function that minimizes the impact of side-channel information. This innovative approach enables us to design a zero-knowledge learning protocol that proves the correctness of our robust cross-domain loss function using a trusted third party. Furthermore, we propose an efficient, practical scheme called robust projection gradient descent (r-PGD) that operates without the need for a trusted third party. By applying r-PGD to various non-linear teacher models, we demonstrate its effectiveness in protecting against model stealing attacks.

We demonstrate that, because the ocean's heat transport has limited range, any variation in the solar radiation must be balanced by changes in the atmosphere's heat capacity, mediated by temperature-dependent latent gas properties. By analyzing this mechanism, we find that the planet's temperature homeostasis is lost when the water vapor in the atmosphere reaches a saturation point, resulting in an increase in high-level clouds that reduce the long-wave radiation and diminish the ocean's heat export.  This breakdown is found to be the underlying cause of the recent rapid warming, as well as the superintense evaporation and carbon cycle fluctuations observed during this period, and it is projected to continue through the remainder of the Century under RCP2.6 and RCP8.5 emission scenarios.  However, our findings also indicate that the planet's temperature homeostosis will be restored in the Year 2230 under the RCP2.6 scenario and in the Year 2370 under the RCP8.5 scenario, regardless of the degree of warming.

This type of perturbation occurs due to the violation of the standard adiabatic condition during the early universe, and it affects the primordial power spectrum of the scalar field. As a result, it modifies the standard nearly-scale-invariant adiabatic pattern, including the amplitude of the scalar gravitational-wave background. The amplitude of these gravitational waves can be significant enough to be measured by next-generation gravitational wave detectors. We develop a new method to relate the amplitude of the scalar gravitational-wave background to the amplitude of the primordial power spectrum of the scalar field. Based on our analysis, we find that the scalar gravitational-wave background can have an amplitude of $2.6\times 10^{-16}$ or an order of magnitude higher when measured in the frequency band of next-generation gravitational wave detectors. This measurement can be performed by detecting the scalar gravitational-wave background in the $f\approx 10^{-21}$ Hz range. Additionally, we find that the scalar gravitational-wave background can also be measured in the $f\approx 2\times 10^{-21}$ Hz range.

We aim to investigate whether the zeros of the zeta function, when plotted as a function of s, exhibit a consistent and predictable pattern. We explore the problem of assessing the risk associated with decisions made by these systems, even when those decisions are influenced by unknown and potentially malicious factors.  A risk assessment metric is proposed, based on a comprehensive consideration of uncertainty and optimisation principles, that can effectively gauge the risk associated with systems compromised by malicious actors, providing a reliable understanding of the inherent risk within such systems.  A key aspect of this metric is a novel formulation of what we call "inner uncertainty", representing the unknown effects of unknown variables.  We demonstrate the applicability of this metric in an example related to state estimation, and discuss approaches for pragmatically estimating the proposed metric in complex scenarios involving substantial amounts of unknown data.

density with pressure for strongly interacting systems at high energies has been sought. Utilizing QCD's property that the correlation between the energy density and pressure can be quantified at sufficiently high energies, it's been established that the coefficient of this correlation is proportional to the square of the shear viscosity coefficient. As a result, the relationship between energy density and pressure can be expressed in terms of the shear viscosity coefficient and a fundamental constant. This relationship has been applied to find the coefficient of the pressure's contribution to the energy density in systems undergoing rapid expansion. The coefficient was found to be 1.5 times the ratio of specific heats in an ideal gas, with the ratio specific to the type of expansion considered. The pressure's contribution to the energy density was found to be 9/2 (2r - 1) for an expansion that mimics nuclear collisions and (3r - 1)/r for an expansion that mimics quark-gluon plasma's behavior in high-energy collisions. This approach was validated through the use of hadron gas models. The pressure's contribution to the energy density in systems undergoing rapid expansion was found to be in the range 2 to 5, depending on the type of expansion and the particles involved.

the movement of people and objects.  This mobility-induced fluctuation affects robot operation, impacting tasks like scene scanning and navigation. This has significant implications for the transfer learning problem of learning from theory to practice.  We argue that the generalization of learning algorithms from simulation to real-world settings requires a specific form of generalization, which we formulate as the transfer generalization problem.  We then establish a connection between transfer generalization and the difference between the laws governing the simulation and real worlds. We also introduce the concept of an "easy" transfer generalization scenario, where the underlying dynamics of the simulation and real worlds differ by a smoothly varying function.  We show that in this scenario, it is possible to achieve near-optimal performance using a transfer learning algorithm based on Bayesian estimation.  However, our results also indicate that noisy dynamical transitions can prevent the algorithm from achieving optimal performance, which may apply to scenarios involving random nonlinear fluctuations.  We demonstrate the efficacy of the algorithm in scenarios modeling robotic grasping and surgery.

early work, this paper's research is centered on the geometric analysis of Navier-Stokes equations in the context of low-Reynolds-number flows.  It begins by examining the simplifications brought about by low-Reynolds-number conditions and boundary conditions for self-similar flows.  These considerations lead to a characterization of possible self-similar flows and their corresponding features.  The existence of stationary, self-similar solutions is determined for both finite and infinite domain scenarios.  The existence of these solutions, however, comes with a caveat: they are unstable.  A key concept introduced in this paper is the notion of a flow's inertial structure, which distinguishes between dominant and subordinate motions.  It is shown that self-similar flows are defined by their inertial structure, particularly in scenarios involving distinct scales.  An overview of the mathematical underpinnings of this concept is provided.  The final section applies this understanding to inertial structures in both theoretical and real-world scenarios.

detecting fundamental frequency in audio files.  The fundamental frequency, represented as f0, is the underlying frequency that defines the structure of music and speech.  Accurate detection of f0 is essential for subsequent analysis in speech and music, including tone detection, melody extraction and translation, and emotion recognition.  Current state-of-the-art methods use techniques such as dynamic programming and hidden Markov models, but these methods can fail when dealing with complex musical backgrounds or when f0 exceeds the 200 Hz threshold.  Our new model utilizes a deep learning technique called the long short-term memory (LSTM) network that can handle long-term dependencies in music and speech.  We modified the standard LSTM design by adding two modules: a filter-bank module that converts audio input into relevant frequency ranges, and an attention module that enables the model to focus on the most informative regions.  Our model achieved a high accuracy of 93.19% on the MEEI dataset, outperforming the previous best method by 2.41% and establishing a new benchmark.

's theory of gravity through experimental means is highly relevant.  We've developed a method to detect gravitational waves produced by binary black hole mergers in globular clusters using the LISA space telescope.  By simulating a large sample of 10,000 binary black hole mergers within 15 globular clusters located near the galactic center, we can observe the unique signatures that these events leave on the gravitational wave spectrum.  These signatures, which include an anomalous background and individual peaks, can provide a means to study the motion of stars within the galactic center through gravitational waves.  Using this approach, we can measure the binary black hole merger rate within the galactic center with an accuracy of around 3 microroads, even with the influence of noise present in the data.  This method also allows us to determine the distance to the galactic center with an accuracy of around 0.5 percent, as well as the metal content of the stars within the galactic center with an accuracy of around 0.07 in [Fe/H].  This method is most accurate for a binary black hole merger rate of around 60 per year, and may be a powerful tool to test the validity of Einstein's theory of gravity through experimental means.

isy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices, are hindered by programming limitations due to error-prone gate execution. In an effort to overcome this constraint, researchers are investigating machine learning-based methods for quantum circuit development, specifically focusing on optimization techniques to identify efficient circuit implementations for general quantum algorithms. In this study, we take a different approach, leveraging our understanding of how specific algorithms transform into circuits, to establish a direct connection between the algorithm's outcomes and circuit components. We illustrate this concept using three prominent quantum algorithms - Simon's algorithm, Shor's algorithm, and the quantum circuit for preparing a superposition across multiple qubits - and successfully demonstrate improved circuit efficiency through a simple, efficient application of our method. We show that applying this method yields closed-form expressions representing optimal circuit components, facilitating efficient simulation, compilation, and verification. Furthermore, this approach enables the representation of certain circuit components using only linear combinations of known operations, thereby enabling the deployment of our method on current NISQ devices.

Neural Networks (BNNs), benefit from

  diffusion-based prior, resulting in an analytically tractable evidence lower 
  bound (ELBO) objective. We propose a novel, non-diffusion based prior, 
  termed ResNet prior, with a related ELBO objective that still offers 
  analytical tractability. To demonstrate the versatility of this prior, 
  we've successfully integrated it into a range of neural network architectures, 
  including deep Q-networks and reinforcement learning agents using recurrent 
  neural networks. Our results show that the ResNet prior can enhance performance 
  and promote more stable training habits, also showcasing benefits in 
  transfer learning and robustness assessments. Notably, we've observed that 
  BNNs trained with the standard prior may exhibit poor performance when 
  encountering new tasks, in contrast to the improved generalization achieved 
  with the ResNet prior. With a detailed analysis of the posterior 
  distribution, we found that the ResNet prior facilitates more output 
  regularization and a broader posterior distribution, both key generalization-
  enhancing factors.

the atomic level is central to various fields like physics and engineering.  This material science branch is known as atomistic modelling and is used to study materials in scenarios that are difficult to replicate in laboratory settings.  One widely used methodology in atomistic modelling is based on the cluster expansion method, but it lacks a comprehensive theoretical basis.  This study derives a more comprehensive framework that includes pairwise and multi-body interactions, making it suitable for describing various phase transition phenomena in materials.  The proposed approach involves expressing atomic interactions through irreducible symmetry groups and their corresponding characters, enabling effective handling of complicated crystal lattices.  The created method, named ONION2, allows for in-silico investigation of materials with complex structures and can be used to study a wide range of materials in atomistic modelling.

Although previous studies have examined the sequential structure of language from various angles, including temporal relationships and discourse implications, they have largely been isolated. the human brain has been hindered by the complexity of its structure. In order to overcome this difficulty, we undertook a comprehensive analysis of the brain's connectivity matrix, which revealed a distinct separation between its intrinsic and extrinsic components. The intrinsic features of the brain's connectivity can be categorized into three primary modes of function, including a universal mode inherent to all regions, a regional mode tied to specific areas, and a global mode associated with hemispheres. Conversely, the extrinsic features reveal a sharp distinction between the two hemispheres, with specific, localized connections that define the network's architecture. Our findings provide a simplified, three-dimensional representation of the brain's connectivity, which may underpin its intricate functional properties and offer a foundation for future studies on the brain's relationships with sensory organs and the body as a whole.

Current automatic evaluation tools, such as the Mean Average Precision (MAP), are ineffective at identifying poor-quality videos, especially when they only comprise a small proportion of the total dataset. In response, we introduce Video-MAP, a more advanced metric that can accurately identify low-quality videos at scale. Our approach involves multi-head attention and a hidden-state based average precision calculation, which enables it to efficiently process large datasets. Experiments demonstrating the effectiveness of Video-MAP, as well as additional metrics such as multi-head attention average precision (MHAP), hidden-state based average precision (HSAP), and their combination (Video-MAP-v2), can be found within this paper. Our results show that these methods yield superior performance, according to human annotations, in comparison to standard average precision metrics. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that Video-MAP's predictive accuracy is linearly correlated with human annotations, outperforming baseline models by up to a 10% absolute gap in low-quality video detection.

Since the field of programming languages continually evolves, it is essential to have a clear and concise way of describing each language to avoid confusion and ambiguity. of electron jets in radio-quiet Active Galactic Nuclei, using multi-wavelength data from NuSTAR, Swift and Gemini.  By analyzing the spectral energy distributions, we find that the electron jets produce an infrared to X-ray component, dominated by synchrotron emission, along with an upper limit on gamma-ray flux of 3% of the jet's total energy.  Comparing this to the jet's power, we determine that the fraction of energy in the gamma-ray component is less than 10%. This sudden change can lead to non-equilibrium effects in species interactions, making it essential to consider the broader community impact. Current mathematical models often isolate specific interactions yet fail to capture the varied impacts of fluctuating environmental conditions. Our research mitigates this limitation by developing a set of stochastic models that can simulate abrupt climate shifts and their consequences on community dynamics. This study focuses on developing an efficient method to calculate the reliability of uncapacitated transportation networks in the presence of random disruptions.  By representing all possible path combinations between origin-destination pairs as a reliability network, we can determine the reliability of the original transportation network.  The size of this reliability network is typically substantial; therefore, we developed an accelerated methodology to analyze its reliability.  This method involves identifying a smaller, high-reliability subset of the original network's paths, and demonstrating that it maintains a significantly similar reliability percentage as the original network.  We also established a mathematical proof of the convergence rate of this subset's reliability proportion as the number of paths in the original network increases.  This research can be applied to various transportation modes, including road, air, and rail.  However, we only tested and presented results for an uncapacitated city block model representing last-mile pedestrian traffic.  Further research is needed to explore other types of transportation networks and determine the optimal threshold for defining the reliability network's path subset.

This study introduces a new approach called the fault-tolerant dynamic output control (FTDOC) that utilizes a robust dynamic output control method to address actuator failures. The FTDOC approach assumes that actuator faults can be modeled as external disturbances within a known bound. The performance of the FTDOC is evaluated under different scenarios, including perfect and imperfect state feedback, as well as various fault types. The results show that the FTDOC leads to stable closed-loop systems and achieves the best possible disturbance rejection effect when there are no delays in feedback signals. The FTDOC is particularly effective in preventing system divergence resulting from prolonged actuator failures. The performance of the FTDOC is illustrated through numerical examples.

This system is chosen because its dissipative behavior can be accurately simulated using a quantum-limited amplifier. When the qubit interacts with the cavity, the observed outcomes are a stochastically varied state and a loss of coherence. Notably, these effects become minimized in a situation called anti-kickboarding, which arises when the qubit attempts to emit photons at the same time as it decays. For anti-kickboarding conditions, our findings show that the system's coherence can be preserved through a feedback process involving the amplifier, enabling the recovery of lost coherence and the successful execution of single-qubit projects, even in the presence of abundant classical noise. Furthermore, this feedback process can also facilitate the successful execution of single-qubit projects, such as rotations, when the anti-kickboarding condition is not met.

machine is trained on a diverse set of images labeled as belonging to specific categories, with the goal of determining whether the algorithm develops unsound generalizations.  We define unsound generalizations as predictions made by the machine that are unlikely to be made by a typical image within a particular category.  Our research involves assessing the occurrence of these predictions on new, unseen images.  We assess our findings using a dataset of high-resolution animal images, along with a dataset of compressed images, both in relation to the use of EfficientNet algorithm.  Our key discoveries indicate that all deep learning algorithms develop unsound generalizations as soon as they achieve high accuracy on a test set.  We further found that there is an inverse correlation between the accuracy of the machine on a test set and the likelihood that it will predict an image as belonging to a particular category when the image actually does not.  We attribute this to over-representation of outliers within each category during the training process.  We found that by training the machine on compressed images, which reduces the amount of data required for training, we can decrease the occurrence of unsound generalizations at the cost of a small decrease in test accuracy.  Our research has implications for the development of more reliable image classification algorithms that are less prone to making unsound generalizations.

studying locally compact groups. They enable us to deduce information about groups using their first-order properties, similar to how model theory applies to abstract groups. This paper specifically examines the relationship between profinite equations and locally compact groups with a trivial intersection of conjugate subgroups, revealing that such groups are precisely those whose profinite counterparts satisfy a certain type of profinite equation. As a consequence, we prove that a locally compact group has a certain property if and only if its profinite counterparts satisfy a specific set of profinite equations, which we do by drawing on both algebraic and model-theoretic techniques. This approach also leads to new inferences about locally compact groups through their connection to profinite counterparts. As an example, we establish that a locally compact group has a compact quotient that is abelian if and only if its profinite counterparts have a certain property, which in turn enables us to deduce that such groups are residually compact.

approach for simulating complex systems that cannot be effectively modeled using conventional Monte Carlo techniques. This method involves introducing a set of auxiliary variables to a system defined by an equilibrium path integral, whose underlying path space is modified to ensure that the probability distribution remains valid even in the presence of system singularities. Once the equilibrium configuration is reached, the auxiliary variables are discarded, and the original system parameters are used for analysis. This review focuses on an overview of the complex Langevin method, including its algorithm, thermal behavior, and how thermal equilibrium is reached. We also examine various applications of the complex Langevin method in the context of quantum field systems that cannot be handled using conventional Monte Carlo techniques. These applications include systems with a single plaquette, geometric scaling, Anomaly, and the presence of monopoles, all within the context of SU(N) gauge models that cannot effectively utilize the conventional minimum action principle due to the presence of singularities.

While the Standard Model successfully explains many phenomena, it leaves some questions unanswered and doesn't include certain fundamental particles, such as neutrinos, which likely have non-zero masses depending on additional interactions.  To extend the Standard Model, one approach is to add right-handed neutrinos to create a mechanism for generating neutrino masses.  Another strategy involves introducing new bosons that could participate in rare processes like rare meson decays or lepton-flavor violation, such as $\mu \to e\gamma$.  To organize these extensions, we recommend utilizing discrete symmetries to restrict the allowed interactions, which in turn can make these models more testable and actionable.  By applying these principles to various extensions of the Standard Model, we aim to identify the theoretical frameworks that could be validated through upcoming experiments.

motion estimation has been a fundamental component 
  in video compression for a long time. Despite widespread use, the p-frame estimation 
  process remains computationally intensive. This paper delves into an alternative, 
  semi-optimal strategy for p-frame estimation, dividing frames into two categories 
  based on motion characteristics. A preliminary experiment involving a widely adopted 
  video codec was modified to add a second prediction frame type, resulting in a p-frame 
  estimation reduction of up to 7.7 times. This optimization appears to be motion 
  independent, suggesting its applicability across diverse video content.

nucleus and proton are well-represented by the color glass condensate, a system characterized by high-density, yet uniformly aligned microscopic connections between particles. In such a system, the alignment of partons within the nucleus and proton results in consistently high levels of gluon momentum sharing among all particles. However, research has shown that the alignment of partons in heavy ions collisions is less consistent due to the variation of initial conditions across different regions of the collision. In the present work, we compare pA collisions to heavy ion collisions, specifically considering the impact of the alignment of partons on phenomena such as jet quenching and gluon momentum sharing. Our research suggests that the larger internal structure of the proton and nucleus makes jet quenching and gluon momentum sharing generally higher in pA collisions than in heavy ions. However, the increase in jet quenching in pA collisions is hindered by the full, unwound flavor structure of partons, while the increase in gluon momentum sharing is further influenced by the distinct flavors of partons due to their uniformly high levels of alignment.

objects in images is a fundamental task in
computer vision with numerous applications, including robot safety and automated
vehicle navigation. Object locations can be considered reliable if they are
consistent across different views of the same scene. This consensus can be
achieved by aligning 2D bounding box correspondences. Existing methods
focus on pairing 2D bounding boxes based on their similarity, but this approach
has its limitations due to the ambiguity in matching objects of varying sizes
and orientations. Instead, we propose Direct Deep Scene Flow by bypassing the
pairing step and directly mapping 2D feature vectors. Our model incorporates
orientation-agnostic features that enable robust alignments. We evaluate our method
at the level of individual objects and also assess its performance in predicting
object correspondences across views. Our results show that DD SF achieves state-
of-the-art accuracy in object location and correspondence tasks, outperforming
previous methods by a significant margin.

The effect of the latter on the solar cell's efficiency remains unclear despite its significance.  Our study involves simulating the interaction between electrons and holes in the gamma phase of CH3NH3KBi2I7 using a non-adabatic Gaussian cube method, which reveals that the electron-hole pair lifetime is length-dependent, ranging from approximately 100 picoseconds in the isolated state to as short as 0.1 picoseconds within the crystal's unit cell.  We find that fast Auger recombination dominates in the isolated pair state, whereas in the crystal, a combination of a lower zero-energy threshold and a weaker coupling to the phonon leads to a longer lifetime.  The result also highlights the importance of further research into the electron-hole interaction and suggests that perovskite solar cells may still operate efficiently despite their short charge carrier lifetime.

studied under dynamic conditions to examine how varying catalyst amounts affect their viscoelastic properties and bond structure, as well as the surface and mechanical properties of hardened materials.  The experiment involved adding different amounts of catalyst to polyurethane components and mixing them at room temperature before subjecting the mixture to shear forces that cause hardening.  The study used an MCR 501 rotational rheometer to measure the viscoelastic properties of the mixture as it hardened under dynamic conditions, and analyze how these properties change over time.  The findings indicate that increasing catalyst amounts leads to a shorter gelation period, but also results in decreased ultimate torque and a slower approach to equilibrium.  The surface and mechanical properties of the materials, analyzed using contact angle and impact strength measurements, showed that increasing catalyst amounts generally lead to tougher surfaces with intermediate hydrophilicity.  The study's results provide a deeper understanding of how catalyst amounts affect the viscoelastic properties and bond structure, surface, and mechanical properties of thermosetting polyurethanes under dynamic conditions.

  The size of these droplets dictates their method of dispersal and where they settle,
  influencing infection risk.  Modeling these droplets as rigid spheres allows tracking
  their trajectory; however, the forces generated by aerodynamic resistance and gravity
  cause them to settle at a rate influenced by their size.  By accounting for the
  force of gravity and potential air currents, we can determine the transmission dynamics.
  Our computational analysis uses a set of interacting Brownian particles to model this
  process and compares the results to laboratory data on droplet settling.  Our findings
  indicate that considering the forces of gravity and air resistance is essential for
  accurately modeling the spread of these droplets.

neural networks has prompted the development of novel computing methods that mimic the human brain. Neuromorphic computing technology, which is particularly suited for handling massive parallelizations, has shown significant potential in optimizing deep model performance. To address the high energy consumption associated with extensive numerical calculations, we have designed a unique, open-source framework called Flexible Neuro-Synaptic Framework (FlexNSF). This framework, which can operate on a single Linux device, leverages the processing capabilities of Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) to enhance the energy efficiency of neural networks. By seamlessly integrating the use of FPGAs and the Python programming language, Python can be used to manage data communication between the FPGA and host device, thereby providing a flexible and efficient neuro-synaptic computing platform. We have utilized this framework to optimize the energy efficiency of neural networks and achieved notable improvements; for example, our research demonstrates that the convolutional neural network model used in the ImageNet dataset only requires approximately 2 megabytes of FPGA memory and achieves a significant reduction of around 75 times in energy consumption compared to traditional GPU computing methods.

has become a fundamental part of modern healthcare, and as a highly sensitive information, its security is a pressing concern. EHR security relies heavily on access control mechanisms that determine which users can view or modify health information. Given the high stakes of misconfigured access, it is essential to analyze the complexity of access control in EHR systems. We have developed a suite of tools to automate the analysis of access control in EHR systems, and our results show that certain configurations are vulnerable to attacks that can bypass security restrictions, potentially allowing unauthorized access to sensitive information. Our research demonstrates that a significant proportion of EHR systems' access control models contain vulnerabilities, and the only known solution to mitigate these vulnerabilities is to significantly restrict the systems' functionality, as the problem is inherently decidable but involves complex computations in practice. Our study also identifies factors that contribute to vulnerabilities in EHR systems' access control, and our findings indicate that certain industry-standard best practices may actually increase the risk of these vulnerabilities.

  This work expresses the H$_\infty$ control problem as an optimal output

  solution in terms of the system's dynamics. The expression also enables
  us to explore different algorithms, such as the Hilbert space-based method,
  and prove its correctness. The study's findings can be applied to a range
  of uncertain systems, including those with time-varying and parametric
  uncertainties. Several examples are provided to illustrate the proposed
  approach's effectiveness.

PyFR, a popular open-source finite rate of spread code, has been refined to accommodate various types of boundary conditions including passive scalar advection at borders. This updated version has been tested on a range of scenarios: resolving the FRS by fixing temperatures below a specified threshold, modeling the relaxation of an initially uniform hot patch of forest fires within a circular area, and simulating the spread of a fire driven by wind. A more precise method of resolving the stencil in PyFR 1.6.0 has been evaluated for its performance. This study compares PyFR 1.6.0 results against a simplified, slower version of the code. Both test cases involved relatively simple scenarios. A larger, more complex scenario was also considered. This scenario differes from the smaller test cases in that it does not settle on a steady, oscillation-free pattern.

To facilitate data efficiency, a typical approach involves introducing similarities between closely timed events. However, the extensive availability of unconnected events in datasets poses a problem known as the "sparsity issue." Our innovative method addresses this issue by combining graph attention networks with contrastive learning, aiming to resolve the sparsity issue and capture event similarities. Our proposed method outperforms other techniques in the sequences and graph domains, according to our experimental findings.

known as Gelfand-Zak orbits or monoids has been extensively studied in relation to Poisson brackets and deformation quantization, revealing a significant association with certain types of quadratic forms, particularly those belonging to the parabolic family. Our research focuses on an often-overlooked subset of these monoids, specifically tailored for a given Poisson bracket, which we term'standard Gelfand-Zak solids.' By establishing a direct connection between these standard Gelfand-Zak solids and the given Poisson bracket's action on a specific type of function, known as the 'central functions,' we are able to develop a criterion for determining whether a certain type of function set constitutes a standard Gelfand-Zak solid. This, in turn, allows us to prove that such function sets of a specific type are closed under the given Poisson bracket action if and only if they are algebraically independent. This finding is particularly significant in the context of the noncommutative Yang-Mills exactness conjecture.

This power spectrum can be divided into two components: a background of 98% representing many identical peaks, and 2% of the mass in high-curvature regions. positions play a crucial role in solving boundary value problems for nonhomogeneous equations. Unlike the case of homogeneous equations, there is no universal formula to express these coefficients. Instead, the coefficients are determined through a system of algebraic equations derived from the given boundary conditions and Fourier transforms of the equation and its solution. Purpose: The purpose of this study is to establish a general method for determining these coefficients using a specific boundary value problem as an example. Methods: We examine a boundary value problem consisting of a time-fractional differential equation and its boundary conditions. By applying the Fourier transform to the equation and obtaining the resulting algebraic system, we then determine the coefficients of the Fourier decompositions. Results: The coefficients we obtain can be expressed as a product of two factors, where one factor is a function of the equation's parameters and the other is a function of the boundary conditions' parameters. The function of the equation's parameters can be expressed in a closed form, whereas the function of the boundary conditions' parameters requires a series solution. The series solution is obtained by using the inverse of an operator that meets specific criteria. Conclusion: The method we present can be used to solve a wide range of boundary value problems by determining the coefficients of the Fourier decompositions of the solution's initial conditions.

One significant capability of these models involves establishing structural relationships between words with similar meanings. Perot cavity is integrated with an optomechanical system to monitor the mechanical properties of a nanoresonator.  We have developed a technique for stabilizing the cavity, which involves linking the cavity's transmission spectrum to a feedback system controlled by the carrier frequency.  By maintaining a small mismatch between the cavity and light source, we can stabilize the cavity even in the presence of high fluctuations.  This stabilization enables precise measurements of the mechanical motion within the cavity.  Using a fiber-optic system, we have demonstrated stabilization of the cavity, achieving a reduction of around 20 times in the mechanical coherence time.  Furthermore, we have successfully adapted this technique to our optomechanical system, achieving a significant improvement of around 50 times in the mechanical coherence time.  This advancement is particularly beneficial for monitoring the mechanical properties of the resonator over an extended period.  We have also demonstrated the ability to measure the mechanical motion within the cavity even when the cavity's transmission spectrum is highly affected by fluctuations.  This is because the feedback system allows us to maintain a stable cavity conditions despite the impact of fluctuations on the transmission spectrum.  Consequently, we can monitor the mechanical motion regardless of the fluctuations' effect on the transmission spectrum.  This strategy is versatile and can be applied to various setups, making it an important technique for optomechanics research.

a successful ensemble learning technique for improving the stability of neural networks.  By combining multiple model training runs with different randomizations, bagging significantly reduces overfitting and makes the network more robust.  We investigated the effectiveness of bagging in training neural networks from scratch and found that it has a limited impact on training deep learning models with significant data.  Interestingly, we discovered that bagging can substantially improve the performance of weak machine learning models, such as those trained on relatively small data sets with robust linear features or those trained using a linear regression model with robust regularization.  We further found that ensemble methods can achieve better results than bagging by minimizing the optimization problem across all models, and we developed an efficient algorithm to solve this problem.  Our experiments confirmed that this algorithm yields high-performance models.  We also introduced an alternative method using bagging that is simpler and more intuitive, and our results showed that it is equally effective.

This occurs when the algorithm makes significant, unforeseen jumps in its policy space, often resulting in the model becoming unstable and producing erratic behavior.  A major contributing factor to overextrapolation is an excessive variance in the estimated action values, which can be attributed to two root causes: 1)  var(V) - the inherent dispersion of the estimated action values, 2)  var(Q) - the unpredictability of estimating action values itself.  To tackle overextraction, the concept of a Reliable Action Explorer (RAE) is introduced.  This modifies the policy update rule to incorporate a reliable proxy for the estimated action values, thereby developing the Reliable Action Explorer (RAE) algorithm.  RAE is shown to mitigate overextrapolation by minimizing the unconditioned variance of the estimated action values.  A new expression for calculating the unconditioned variance of action values is derived and found to consist of two components:  the inherent dispersion of the action values and the unpredictability of estimating those action values. While research has been done on the growth of diamond crystals using microwave energy, this study takes it a step further by utilizing a high-power microwave cavity to examine the effects on diamond properties.  By comparing samples grown with and without the cavity, our findings show that loading the cavity with diamond results in a significant enhancement of the conduction loss at high frequencies, outpacing the rate of energy absorption through the Faraday rotation effect.  Moreover, we discovered that growing diamond within the cavity significantly reduces boron incorporation, yielding a narrow band of microwave frequencies with the lowest loss values (specifically, 19.3 GHz with a corresponding loss value of 2.5 x 10^-3).  Scanning electron microscopy images reveal that growing diamond within the cavity reduces the size of nitrogen-vacancy defects and facilitates the aggregation of voids into larger particles. organic metal $\kappa$-($\eta$)Hg[${\eta}$-C$_5$H$_5$N$_5$] were investigated using magnetic susceptibility measurements in field strengths ranging from 0.1 T to 3.5 T and temperatures from 1.9 K to 300 K.  The overall structure of the mercury compound is composed of a two-dimensional metal grid interspersed with the N$_5$ radical anion in both its $\eta$ and $\eta$ forms.  The measured magnetic susceptibility showed the expected Curie law behavior at higher temperatures, while at lower temperatures it exhibited an enhancement of the magnetic moment due to intermolecular antiferromagnetic interactions.  The results suggest that the compound is an intrinsically three-dimensional antiferromagnet with a weak exchange interaction.  Additionally, the measured susceptibility in a magnetic field showed the expected decrease in the magnetic moment as the field strength increased, indicating that the antiferromagnetic behavior could be reversed with a sufficiently strong magnetic field.  The magnetic properties of the $\eta$ form of the mercury compound are essentially the same as those of the $\eta$ form, with the difference being a slight variation in the intensity of the antiferromagnetic behavior depending on the configuration of the N$_5$ radical anions.

The environment responds immediately to the agent's actions with a reward signal, but doesn't accommodate external observations. We investigate two types of feedback: bandit feedback, which provides individualized reward information, and online learning with bandit feedback's opposite, where the agent receives the same reward information for all actions taken at a given time step. We explored two types of feedback scenarios: online learning with bandit feedback, online learning without differentiation of rewards. We developed an overarching framework that unifies these settings and established a representative model. We analyzed the general framework's performance and derived a regret bound. The regret measure assesses the difference between the agent's cumulative rewards and the optimal achievable reward in an offline setting. The obtained regret bound incorporates terms based on the number of time steps, actions, and action combinations. have revolutionized natural language processing tasks by leveraging contextual representations. These models selectively share knowledge with neighboring words through a rich token-based embedding table. Unlike contextual representations in unsupervised neural language models, the learned representations in PLMs are supervised and therefore more effective. It has been observed that merely replacing the token-based with a weighted sum of the hidden states can significantly impair performance. This suggests that the conventional positional embedding table used in transformer-based PLMs is more than just a sophisticated zero-fill operation. To further optimize the hybrid architecture comprising both global and local mechanisms, research on contextual representations should delve deeper into the understanding of the neural network architecture, supervision, and learning dynamics. To this end, our analysis highlights the inherent over-parametrization in the conventional transformer-based PLMs, where the global mechanism is an explicit positional feedback loop, effectively turning the hybrid architecture into a unified multi-head attention mechanism. Moreover, our findings suggest that the conventional configuration is already optimizing a weighted sum of the input sequences' contextual representations, thereby providing a theoretical basis for the effectiveness of the embeddings. This understanding is illustrated through a simplified, open-source framework that can be applied to any transformer-based language model, offering a set of best practices for the development of future models.

While nitrogen-vacancy defects in diamond have undergone extensive study, the optical signatures of vacancy defects in 3C-SiC, particularly when combined with nitrogen, have not been thoroughly examined despite this material's widespread use. This paper delves into the details of a study that assessed the effect of a lottery-based incentive program on the take-up rate of a crucial public benefit. The authors discovered that participants selected for the incentive program were significantly more likely to claim the benefit, with the difference being particularly pronounced among low-probability winners.   Developing high-quality, automatic translation tools has been a subject of research
  and debate in the NLP community for over a decade. Advanced neural network-based
  models, particularly the sequence-to-sequence model, have been successfully
  employed in MT. However, translating certain sentences, particularly those that

  we thoroughly examine and evaluate multiple techniques for OOV handling in MT,

thermal properties of complex networks comprised of interconnecting subgraphs, referred to as 'pegs'. The 'peg's' structure can be broadly categorized into two types: transversal and non-transversal configurations. A transversal peg corresponds to a unique combination of mutually exclusive pairs of disjoint sets, thereby ensuring a precise and straightforward calculation of its thermal characteristics. Conversely, a non-transversal peg necessitates a more intricate 'backtracking' algorithm to determine its structural composition, which in turn affects the computation of its thermal properties. Our model encompasses a wide range of network structures, including those represented by specific exponential and power-law degree distributions. Additionally, we explore the general framework for the thermal properties of pegs, focusing particularly on the average degree and its variation across the network. Our findings are expected to contribute to a broader understanding of the relationship between network structure and its thermal properties.

erial Vehicles (UAVs) is projected to reach $14.9 billion by 2025, driven by growing demand for remote sensing technology. To address this issue, we have developed an automated system for validating no-fly zones (NFZs) in Australia, which are currently undefined in our dataset. By analyzing safety-related data from the Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA), we can categorize and quantify NFZs and thereby make flight planning more efficient. The appearance of a spin-resonance peak in the magnetic susceptibility is investigated as the temperature is raised from zero. Our results are based on an exact diagrammatic expansion that includes the influence of the pair field on the spin-resonance peak. The impact of pairing on the width and position of the spin-resonance peak is calculated and found to be significant, differing substantially from predictions made without considering the pair field's effect. The width of the spin-resonance peak is found to be much broader than expected at higher temperatures due to the decomposition of the collective mode into pair and single-particle excitations. The accuracy of our results is ensured by comparison with Monte Carlo simulations and other theoretical models. The development of the spin-resonance peak is charted over temperature, and the influence of pairing on the spin-resonance peak is contrasted with that of a simple interaction. The composition of the spin-resonance peak, whether it arises from the (γ, n) or (γ, p) reaction, is also determined.

Stochastic Convergence for Random Fields has been established under the conditions of the Riemann-Zurich problem. This involves demonstrating that for a stable random field $X$ defined on a $d$-dimensional domain $D$, whose values are in the interval $[0,1]$, and for any stable index $\alpha$ (where $1 < \alpha \leq 2$) and small positive value $h$, the probability that the difference between $X$ and its rescaled minimum value, $X_h$, is less than $h$ tends towards zero as the dimension of $D$ is greater than $\alpha$. This, in turn, shows that the boundary of the set where $X$ attains its minimum value has an area of zero. The case of fractional fields, where the index $\alpha$ is a fraction with $2$ as the denominator, is also considered, and it is shown that the probability that the difference between $X$ and its rescaled minimum value, $X_h$, is less than $h$ tends towards a value of $e^{-1/(Ch^\alpha)}$ as $h$ approaches zero. This is further illustrated by the specific example of an isotropic Gaussian field.

protein structure prediction, a critical task in molecular biology. Recent advancements in alpha-helices and beta-sheets prediction have been promising, but predicting the overall global structure of a protein remains challenging.
